title: Integer weight decomposition of rational multiplicative-group representations
statement: Let $k$ be any field [def-weil-field], let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space, and let $\rho:\mathbf G_{m,k}\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a homomorphism of $k$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme], where $\mathbf G_m$ is the multiplicative group of [def-sc-gm-ga] and $\operatorname{GL}(V)(R)=\operatorname{Aut}_R(V\otimes_kR)$ for a commutative $k$-algebra $R$. Equivalently the representation is specified by a linear coaction $c:V\to V\otimes_k k[t,t^{-1}]$ satisfying coassociativity and the counit identity for $\Delta(t)=t\otimes t$, $\epsilon(t)=1$. For $a\in\mathbf Z$ put $V_a=\{v:c(v)=v\otimes t^a\}$. Then $V=\bigoplus_{a\in\mathbf Z}V_a$, with only finitely many nonzero summands. In particular $V$ has an ordered basis $e_1,\ldots,e_s$ and integers $a_1,\ldots,a_s$ such that $\rho_R(z)e_i=z^{a_i}e_i$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $R$ and $z\in R^\times$. The decomposition and basis assertion hold in every characteristic, including $\dim V=0$.

proof.text: Put $A=k[t,t^{-1}]$. First make the representation/coaction dictionary and its evaluation explicit. Apply [lem-sfb-hopf-coaction-linearization] to $H=\mathbf G_m$, $E=k$ with its trivial action and $M=V$. Its linearization is an $A$-linear automorphism of $V\otimes_k A$, its restriction to $v\otimes1$ is $c(v)$, and its identity and composition identities are precisely the counit and coassociativity identities. For a $k$-algebra $R$ and $z\in R^\times$, pull this automorphism back along $\operatorname{ev}_z:A\to R$, $t\mapsto z$. It sends $v\otimes1$ to $(1\otimes\operatorname{ev}_z)c(v)$. Pulling the composition identity back along $(z,w)$ gives $\rho_R(z)\rho_R(w)=\rho_R(zw)$; its inverse is evaluation at $z^{-1}$. Conversely a group-scheme representation evaluated at the universal point $t\in A^\times$ gives this linearization, with the same identities, and hence its coaction. These constructions are inverse: every $z$ is the image of $t$ under $\operatorname{ev}_z$. Thus the formula holds for the given representation on every test algebra.

proof.text: For each $a\in\mathbf Z$, let $\lambda_a:A\to k$ take the coefficient of $t^a$. The finite, unique Laurent expansion in [def-weil-laurent-polynomial-ring] makes $\lambda_a$ linear and gives $\lambda_a(t^b)=\delta_{ab}$. The tensor universal property [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] gives, for every $k$-module $M$, a linear map $E_a:M\otimes_k A\to M$, $m\otimes f\mapsto\lambda_a(f)m$. Each tensor $x$ has a unique finite expansion $x=\sum_aE_a(x)\otimes t^a$: expand its finitely many pure-tensor summands in Laurent monomials for existence and apply $E_b$ for uniqueness. Write $p_a=E_a\circ c$. Then $p_a:V\to V$ is linear, $c(v)=\sum_a p_a(v)\otimes t^a$, and every $v$ has finite support. In subsequent formulas use the tensor unit map $M\otimes k\to M$, $m\otimes r\mapsto rm$, inverse $m\mapsto m\otimes1$, and the reassociation map $(M\otimes A)\otimes A\to M\otimes(A\otimes A)$ sending $(m\otimes f)\otimes g$ to $m\otimes(f\otimes g)$. The reverse formula is its inverse, since pure tensors generate. All these maps follow directly from the same universal property.

source.place: Theorem 12.12(a) ⇒ (b) and (d), Remark 12.13, printed pp.234–235; coefficient argument specialized to G_m

proof.text:
Coassociativity and $\Delta(t^a)=t^a\otimes t^a$ give the finite-sum identity
$$\sum_a c(p_a(v))\otimes t^a=\sum_a p_a(v)\otimes t^a\otimes t^a.$$
Apply extraction of the last Laurent coefficient $b$, using step 2 with $M=V\otimes_k A$. It gives $c(p_b(v))=p_b(v)\otimes t^b$, so $p_b(v)\in V_b$. Applying $1\otimes\epsilon$ to the expansion of $c(v)$, with $\epsilon(t^a)=1$, gives $v=\sum_a p_a(v)$. Thus every vector is a finite sum of weight vectors.

source.place: Theorem 12.12(a) ⇒ (b) and (d), Remark 12.13, printed pp.234–235; coefficient argument specialized to G_m

proof.text: If $w\in V_a$, its defining equation $c(w)=w\otimes t^a$ and coefficient extraction give $p_b(w)=\delta_{ab}w$. Each $V_a$ is a subspace, since its defining equation is linear. For a finite relation $\sum_a w_a=0$ with $w_a\in V_a$, apply $p_b$ to obtain $w_b=0$. Therefore the addition map from the direct sum (finite-support families $(w_a)$, with $w_a\in V_a$) to $V$ is both surjective by step 3 and injective by this calculation. This proves the asserted internal direct sum and its uniqueness.

source.place: Theorem 12.12(a) ⇒ (b) and (d), Remark 12.13, printed pp.234–235; coefficient argument specialized to G_m

proof.text: Choose a finite spanning family $v_1,\ldots,v_r$ of $V$, permitted by [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace]. Let $S\subset\mathbf Z$ be the union of their finite coefficient supports in step 2. If $a\notin S$, then $p_a(v_j)=0$ for every $j$, and linearity implies $p_a=0$ on $V$. But $p_a$ is the identity on $V_a$ by step 4, so $V_a=0$. Further, the finite homogeneous family $(p_a(v_j))_{a\in S,1\le j\le r}$ spans $V$: express $v$ in the $v_j$ and replace each $v_j$ by the finite sum in step 3. Thus only finitely many weights occur, without any assumption on the characteristic or on the number of $k$-points of $\mathbf G_m$.

source.place: Theorem 12.12(a) ⇒ (b) and (d), Remark 12.13, printed pp.234–235; coefficient argument specialized to G_m

proof.text: Scan the finite homogeneous spanning list of step 5 in any order, retaining a vector exactly when it is outside the span of the vectors already retained. At each stage the retained vectors are independent: in a new relation a nonzero coefficient on the last vector would express it in the previous span, since $k$ is a field. A discarded vector is already in that span, so the final retained list still spans $V$. It is therefore an ordered basis $e_1,\ldots,e_s$ in the sense of [def-weil-pbc-free-module], and each $e_i$ retains its integer weight $a_i$. Zero vectors are discarded automatically. If $V=0$, no vector is retained and this is the empty ordered basis.

source.place: Theorem 12.12(a) ⇒ (b) and (d), Remark 12.13, printed pp.234–235; coefficient argument specialized to G_m

proof.text: For every commutative $k$-algebra $R$ and $z\in R^\times$, evaluate $c(e_i)=e_i\otimes t^{a_i}$ using step 1 to obtain $\rho_R(z)(e_i\otimes1)=e_i\otimes z^{a_i}$. Here negative powers are defined because $z$ is a unit. The vectors $e_i\otimes1$ form an $R$-basis: extend the $k$-coordinate maps of the basis to $V\otimes_kR$ by $v\otimes r\mapsto r\,e_i^*(v)$, whose inverse sends a tuple $(r_i)$ to $\sum_i e_i\otimes r_i$; the two compositions are identities on basis vectors and pure tensors. This also covers the zero algebra and $s=0$. The claimed formula, usually abbreviating $e_i\otimes1$ to $e_i$, consequently holds over every test algebra.
